Honest
on'est
a. (upright, seemly, of good repute; in the Authorized Version chiefly what is comely and creditable before men as well as before God)
From Latin honestus, honourable, from honos, honour, through Old French honeste. In 1611 English the word still carried its Latin breadth — not merely “not a thief” but honourable, seemly, of good report. The Greek behind it is kalos, beautiful or noble, and semnos, grave and venerable.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses honest where modern speech would say honourable. Our Lord names the soil that bears fruit as “an honest and good heart” (Luke 8:15) — not a heart that has ceased to lie, but a heart made noble, sound, and fit to hold the word. The apostle commands a public quality of life: “Provide things honest in the sight of all men” (Romans 12:17), and again, “Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21). The setting of that second verse is the handling of the Macedonian collection; Paul would not carry other men's money alone, and the deliberate transparency he built into the arrangement is what he calls honest. The word therefore reaches past private integrity into visible, checkable conduct. It enters Paul's catalogue of what the sanctified mind is to dwell upon: “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Philippians 4:8). Peter presses the same thing on strangers in a hostile world — “Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles” (1 Peter 2:12) — so that slander would be refuted by the plain look of the thing. Honesty in Scripture is never merely negative. It is the fruit of a regenerate heart, made visible.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives honest first as upright and just in dealing, then as decent, honourable, and suitable — the broad sense the Authorized Version carries.

expand to see more

HONEST, a. on'est. Upright; just; fair in dealing with others; free from trickishness and fraud; acting and having acted the part of a just man.

2. Fair; just; equitable; free from fraud.

3. Decent; honorable; suitable to the character or station.

4. Frank; sincere; unreserved; as an honest countenance.

HONESTY, n. In principle, an upright disposition; moral rectitude of heart; a disposition to conform to justice and correct moral principles, in all social transactions.

Key Scripture

Luke 8:15 — "But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience."

Romans 12:17 — "Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men."

2 Corinthians 8:21 — "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men."

1 Peter 2:12 — "Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation."

Modern Corruption

Honesty has been shrunk to blunt self-disclosure — “I'm just being honest” — which licenses cruelty and excuses nothing.

expand to see more

The modern use of the word has collapsed into a single narrow act: saying out loud whatever one presently feels. On that reckoning a man is honest when he tells his wife exactly what he thinks of her, and the phrase I'm just being honest becomes a licence rather than a claim. Scripture will not have it. The honest man of Romans 12:17 is the man who provides things honest in the sight of all men — whose accounts, promises, workmanship, and reputation will bear inspection. Blunt speech that wounds without love is not honesty; it is what Proverbs calls the piercing of a sword, and the tongue of the wise is set against it.

The opposite error is equally common in the church: an honesty confined to the heart, invisible to the neighbour, resting on the claim that God alone sees. Paul refuses that too. He arranged the Jerusalem collection so that men as well as the Lord could see the handling of it, because a ministry above suspicion is part of the ministry itself. Where elders, deacons, and treasurers decline that visibility, appealing to their own sincerity, the word honest in its Authorized sense has already been lost. Recover it and much else follows: open books, kept promises, work done when no one is watching, and a reputation that will not have to be defended.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kalos, good or noble — Luke 8:15, Romans 12:17, 1 Peter 2:12; semnos, grave and honourable — Philippians 4:8; agathos, good — Luke 8:15.

expand to see more

Greek kalos — beautiful, noble, of good report; the word rendered honest in Romans 12:17, 2 Corinthians 8:21 and 1 Peter 2:12.

Greek semnos — grave, venerable, worthy of reverence; Philippians 4:8, and the required character of deacons and aged men.

Greek agathos — good in substance; paired with kalos in Luke 8:15, “an honest and good heart.”

Hebrew yashar — straight, upright; the Old Testament root behind the same moral idea, as in Proverbs 11:3.

Latin honestus, from honos, honour — the source of the English word and of its older, broader sense.

Usage

"“An honest and good heart” — the soil that keeps the word and bears fruit with patience."

"“Provide things honest in the sight of all men” — visible, checkable conduct, not private sincerity."

"Paul's handling of the collection: transparency built in beforehand, so that no man could suspect."
